profiles.meeting_scenario: The meeting is an internal design review for a planned replication-and-extension study in an ML/robotics lab. The team is reviewing a proposal for a benchmark paper comparing three controller/learner pairings for modular robots with previously unseen morphologies: CPG + evolutionary search, neural-network controller + evolutionary search, and neural-network controller + RL. The context is that the lab wants to submit a systems-oriented benchmark paper in eight weeks and needs to decide whether the current evaluation design is review-ready. The agenda is to assess whether the proposed benchmark protocol is sufficiently fair, reproducible, and complete for unseen-morphology claims, identify any gaps in the plan, and agree on modifications before implementation starts. The expected outcome is a conditional approval of the design review with a short list of revisions to the evaluation protocol and reporting package.

members.name: Dr. Maya Chen
members.expertise: evolutionary robotics, benchmark design, empirical comparison studies
members.background: Maya leads the lab's embodied ML benchmarking efforts and has previously published comparative studies on controller robustness in simulated modular robots. She is responsible for the scientific framing and for making sure the paper's claims about generality will survive external review.
members.private_state: She wants the design approved quickly so the implementation team can start, but she is especially worried about reviewer criticism around benchmark fairness and about accidentally overclaiming generalization to unseen morphologies.
hidden_assumptions: When the proposal says 'unseen morphologies,' it means the held-out body graphs are never used during any hyperparameter selection or ablation tuning, not merely excluded from final reporting.

A design is 'review-ready' once the evaluation protocol, reporting tables, and statistical treatment are specified tightly enough that implementation choices cannot materially change the paper's claims.

The 'robustness' section naturally includes perturbations applied at evaluation time to already-trained controllers, because robustness is about post-training performance stability rather than training success under noisy conditions.
Using a 'standard budget' across methods means equalizing total simulator interactions at the comparison layer, even if wall-clock usage or number of optimization updates differ internally.

members.name: Alex Romero
members.expertise: reinforcement learning systems, experiment infrastructure, reproducible training pipelines
members.background: Alex owns the experiment stack for robot learning, including simulator integration, job orchestration, and result aggregation. He has shipped several large-scale RL evaluation pipelines and is focused on what can be executed reliably within fixed compute and staffing limits.
members.private_state: He wants the review to end with a practical protocol that can be implemented without exploding compute cost, and he is quietly trying to constrain the scope so the team can finish the benchmark before the submission deadline.
hidden_assumptions: When the proposal says 'unseen morphologies,' it refers to the morphologies excluded from the final benchmark table; using a small held-out subset from that pool during tuning is acceptable as long as those exact instances are not in the final averages.
A design is 'review-ready' once the training pipeline, seeds, logging, and run matrix are concrete enough for engineering execution, even if some reporting choices are refined later.

The 'robustness' section naturally covers variability across random seeds and mild training-time noise injections, because those are the most operationally important failure modes for large experiment runs.
Using a 'standard budget' means equalizing scheduled GPU/CPU compute and wall-clock allocation per method so the benchmark is feasible and resource-fair in practice.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the benchmark should make claims about 'unseen morphologies.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a morphology family that is fully quarantined from all tuning, ablations, and threshold-setting until final evaluation; any contact during model selection contaminates the unseen claim.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means morphologies not included in the final reported test table; using nearby held-out morphologies from the same pool during pipeline tuning is still compatible with calling the final ones 'unseen.'
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase is standard in ML papers and both members think they are invoking a common benchmark norm, so neither feels a need to unpack whether 'unseen' applies only to final reporting or to the entire design loop.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree each method should run under a 'standard budget' for a fair comparison.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks fairness requires equalizing total simulator interaction counts across all three controller/learner combinations because sample efficiency is part of the scientific claim.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks fairness requires equalizing allocated compute time and cluster resources across methods because engineering feasibility and reproducibility depend on wall-clock parity.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In benchmark discussions, 'budget' is routinely used as a shorthand for fairness, and both interpretations sound professionally reasonable, so the phrase creates false consensus unless someone explicitly asks 'budget in what units?'

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the paper needs a 'robustness analysis.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes robustness includes post-training perturbation tests such as actuator dropout, terrain variation, and sensor noise applied to trained controllers on held-out morphologies.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes robustness mainly means stability of outcomes across seeds and limited training-time noise settings already supported by the infrastructure.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Robustness is a broad, overloaded term in embodied ML; both members expect the other to share the common-sense notion without enumerating which perturbation family is inside the review scope.

misalignment_points.topic: Which held-out set they mean by 'the test suite'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to evaluating on 'the test suite' and 'the held-out set.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the 24-morphology final benchmark pack assembled for the paper draft, stratified by limb count and symmetry class.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the 12-morphology engineering validation pack currently configured in the experiment runner, which was built earlier for smoke tests and capacity planning.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both sets are internal artifacts commonly called 'the test suite' in the lab, and because the review focuses on protocol rather than raw file lists, the naming collision sounds harmless and never gets challenged.

turns.inner_thought: I need this approved today, but only if the protocol is tight enough that reviewers can't say we contaminated the unseen-morphologies claim or let implementation drift change the scientific story. For me, review-ready means the evaluation protocol, reporting tables, and stats are locked down now. We also need fairness in terms of equal simulator interaction counts, and robustness has to mean post-training performance under perturbations on truly quarantined held-out body graphs.
